To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) if the Universe is homogeneous on large scales, then the average dynamics is well-described by an FRW cosmology, (ii) if the Universe has a homogeneity length-scale much smaller than the horizon, then the average large-scale dynamics is well-described as an FRW cosmological model, (iii) if the Universe today has a homogeneity scale comparable to the horizon, then we do not know how to answer the question of the effect of averaging on the average dynamics.
(i) the effect of averaging over inhomogenities on the large scale dynamics is negligibly small, and (ii) the scale of homogenity on large scales can be observationally determined.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the average large-scale cosmological dynamics is well described by the standard FLRW model.
the following question: Is there an effect of cosmic inhumogeneities on the large scale average dynamics?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are strong theoretical indications and weak observational evidence that the Universe is homogeneous on large scales, and that the effect of inhomogeneities and averaging is negligible.
there is no compelling evidence yet for a significant effect of back-reaction on large scales, but that the issue is not fully settled yet.
if the Universe is homogeneous on scales much smaller than the current Hubble scale, the effect of back-reaction is small.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the back-reaction effect on the large scale FLRW dynamics is small, if the length scale of homogeneity on which the averaging is performed is much smaller than today's Hubble scale.
we do not have a compelling reason to believe that the average large-scale dynamics of the Universe is significantly different from a homogeneous, isotopic FRW model.
the back-reaction is small, and that the Universe is well-approximated as homogeneous on scales larger than the homogeneity scale.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, if the scale of homogeneities in the Universe is much smaller than today's Hubble radius, the back-reactions from averaging over inhomogeneity is negligible.
the effect of back-reaction is not large even for a scale of homogeneity which is comparable to the Hubblescale today.
the backreaction due to averaging over nonlinear inhomogeneities in the real Universe on large scales is small and hence can be safely ignored in the standard FRW description of the Universe.
